120756.e: The plots are walked along a fixed route and the three groups are counted. They show species diversity at landscape level.
120756.m: On its square-kilometre plots, the BDM counts plants, butterflies and breeding birds.

120757.q: How are the BDM sample plots chosen?
a: In a regular grid across the whole of Switzerland
120757.e: A systematic grid makes sure all landscapes are fairly represented. This way the data reflect the whole of Switzerland, not just special places.
120757.m: A regular grid makes the BDM representative.

120758.q: How often is each BDM sample plot surveyed again?
120758.e: Each year, one fifth of the plots is surveyed. After five years, one round is complete and changes become visible.
120758.m: Each BDM plot is surveyed again every five years.

120759.q: Which trend do the BDM data show for the species communities of many habitats?
a: They are becoming more and more different
They now consist only of neophytes
120759.e: Common, undemanding species are spreading, while specialists are declining. As a result, the communities of different places are becoming increasingly alike.
120759.m: Species communities in Switzerland are becoming more uniform.

120760.q: Which change do the BDM data show for many plant and animal species in connection with climate change?
a: They are increasingly found at higher altitudes
They are moving down to the lowlands
They are disappearing from the Alps
120760.e: As temperatures rise, many species shift their range uphill. Mountain species can come under pressure because the space runs out at the top.
120760.m: Climate change is driving many species uphill.

120761.q: Which institution collects a lot of data on breeding birds in Switzerland and so contributes to monitoring?
a: The Swiss Ornithological Institute in Sempach
The Bern Museum of Fine Arts
120761.e: The Swiss Ornithological Institute in Sempach coordinates counts with many volunteer experts. Its data show how breeding bird populations are developing.
120761.m: The Swiss Ornithological Institute in Sempach keeps watch on Swiss birdlife.

120762.q: What does the category CR on the Red List mean?
120762.e: CR stands for “critically endangered”. It is the highest level of threat before extinction in the wild.
120762.m: CR is the highest threat level.

120763.q: What does the category EW on the Red List mean?
120763.e: EW means “extinct in the wild”. The species survives only in zoos, botanical gardens or breeding programmes.
120763.m: A species listed as EW lives only in human care.

120764.q: Who publishes the national Red Lists in Switzerland?
a: The FOEN together with national data and information centres
120764.e: Specialist centres such as Info Flora or info fauna prepare the assessments. The FOEN publishes the lists as the official basis for nature conservation.
120764.m: The Swiss Red Lists are published by the FOEN.

120765.q: According to the FOEN, what proportion of the species studied in Switzerland are threatened?
120765.e: Switzerland's Red Lists show that about one third of the assessed species are threatened. The main causes are the loss and decline of habitats.
120765.m: In Switzerland, about one third of the species studied are threatened.

120766.q: Which three categories does the IUCN group together as “threatened”?
120766.e: Critically endangered (CR), endangered (EN) and vulnerable (VU) together make up the threatened species. LC means least concern.
120766.m: Threatened species are classed as CR, EN or VU.

120767.q: What does the category DD on the Red List mean?
120767.e: DD stands for “data deficient”. There is not enough information for an assessment, but the species may still be threatened.
120767.m: With DD, data for an assessment are missing.

120768.q: What does the Red List of the International Union for Conservation of Nature (IUCN) show?
a: How strongly animal and plant species are threatened with extinction
Which species are allowed as pets
120768.e: The IUCN Red List assesses worldwide how threatened a species is, from “least concern” to “extinct”. Today it includes more than a hundred thousand assessed species.
120768.m: The Red List shows how strongly species are threatened with extinction.

120769.q: Which volcanic island, formed off Iceland in 1963, is strictly protected as an outdoor laboratory for primary succession?
120769.e: Surtsey formed in an underwater eruption from 1963. Only researchers may set foot on the island, so that its natural colonisation can be observed undisturbed.
120769.m: On Surtsey, scientists observe how a new island is colonised.

120770.q: After which British ecologist is the pyramid of numbers for trophic levels named?
120770.e: In 1927, in “Animal Ecology”, Charles Elton described how the number of individuals usually decreases from level to level. This diagram is called the Eltonian pyramid.
120770.m: The Eltonian pyramid shows the number of animals per trophic level.

120771.q: What does the category RE mean in Switzerland's Red Lists?
120771.e: RE stands for “regionally extinct”. The species has disappeared from Switzerland but still occurs elsewhere.
120771.m: RE means a species has died out in the country concerned.

120772.q: Which shape does the basic Lotka-Volterra model show when the number of predators is plotted against the number of prey?
a: A closed curve around a point of equilibrium
120772.e: In the phase diagram, predators and prey go through the same cycle again and again. The path closes because the process repeats exactly.
120772.m: In the phase diagram, predators and prey form closed cycles.

120773.q: Which co-receptor marks T helper cells on their surface?
120773.e: Because of their surface molecule CD4, T helper cells are also called CD4-positive T cells. The co-receptor stabilises the binding to the antigen-presenting cell.
120773.m: T helper cells are CD4-positive lymphocytes.

120774.q: Which cells show T helper cells fragments of germs so that they become active?
120774.e: Phagocytes take in germs, break them up and present fragments on their surface. When a T helper cell recognises such a fragment, it is activated.
120774.m: T helper cells are activated by antigen-presenting cells.

120775.q: Which virus specifically attacks T helper cells and, if untreated, leads to AIDS?
120775.e: HIV uses the CD4 molecule as a way in and gradually destroys the T helper cells. Without treatment, the immune defence therefore collapses.
120775.m: HIV weakens the immune system by destroying T helper cells.

120776.q: What role do T helper cells play in making antibodies?
a: They activate B cells, which then make antibodies
They have nothing to do with it
120776.e: B cells usually need the help of T helper cells to develop into plasma cells. Only these then produce large amounts of antibodies.
120776.m: T helper cells help B cells to make antibodies.

120777.q: Why are T helper cells also called the “conductors” of the immune system?
a: They coordinate other defence cells with messenger substances
They carry nerve signals to the brain
120777.e: T helper cells release messenger substances that activate phagocytes, B cells and killer cells. In this way they control the whole defence response.
120777.m: T helper cells control the immune defence.

120778.q: Where do T cells mature, which is also what the “T” in their name refers to?
120778.e: T cells are formed in the bone marrow and then mature in the thymus behind the breastbone. There they learn to tell the body's own substances from foreign ones.
120778.m: T cells mature in the thymus.

120779.q: What is the main job of regulatory T cells?
120779.e: Regulatory T cells slow down immune responses that go too far. In this way they help to prevent autoimmune diseases.
120779.m: Regulatory T cells protect the body from excessive immune reactions.

120780.q: Why do people with untreated AIDS fall ill with infections that are harmless for healthy people?
a: They lack the T helper cells that coordinate the defence
They have too many red blood cells
120780.e: HIV gradually destroys the T helper cells. Without them, the control of the defence collapses, and even otherwise harmless germs become dangerous.
120780.m: Without T helper cells, the defence collapses.

120781.q: What are the messenger substances called that immune cells use to communicate with each other?
120781.e: Cytokines such as the interleukins are released by immune cells. They activate other cells, make them multiply or damp down reactions.

120782.q: To which group of white blood cells do cytotoxic T cells belong?
120782.e: T cells and B cells are lymphocytes and form the specific defence. Granulocytes and monocytes belong to the innate defence.

120784.q: What does a cytotoxic T cell trigger in a cell infected with a virus?
a: Healing of the cell through repair
120784.e: The T cell releases substances that start apoptosis in the target cell. The cell dies in an orderly way, and the viruses inside cannot multiply any further.
120784.m: Cytotoxic T cells make diseased cells destroy themselves.

120785.q: Unlike T cells, which immune cells make antibodies?
120785.e: Activated B cells become plasma cells and release antibodies into the blood. Cytotoxic T cells, on the other hand, kill infected cells directly.

120786.q: Which cells are typically killed by cytotoxic T cells?
a: Cells infected with viruses and tumour cells
120786.e: Cytotoxic T cells recognise foreign peptides on the surface of the body's own cells. In this way they get rid of cells in which viruses are multiplying or that have become abnormal.
120786.m: Cytotoxic T cells remove infected and abnormal body cells.

120787.q: What is the aim of immunotherapy against cancer?
a: To activate the body's own immune system against the tumour
To destroy the tumour with radiation
To remove the tumour by surgery
To switch the immune system off completely
120787.e: Tumours can put the brakes on the defence. Immunotherapies release these brakes or prime T cells specifically so that they attack cancer cells.
120787.m: Immunotherapy turns the body's own defence into a cancer fighter.

120788.q: What is CAR T-cell therapy mainly used for?
a: Against certain types of blood cancer
120788.e: In CAR T-cell therapy, the patient's own T cells are genetically fitted with an artificial receptor. Afterwards they specifically recognise cancer cells, for example in certain leukaemias and lymphomas.
120788.m: CAR T-cell therapy turns your own T cells into targeted cancer hunters.

120789.q: How does a cytotoxic T cell recognise a body cell infected with a virus?
a: By foreign protein fragments on its surface
120789.e: Infected cells show fragments of viral proteins on their surface. The T cell recognises these foreign pieces with its receptor.
120789.m: T cells recognise infected cells by foreign protein fragments.

120790.q: Where do B lymphocytes mature in humans?
120790.e: B lymphocytes form and mature in the bone marrow. T lymphocytes, by contrast, mature in the thymus gland.
120790.m: B cells mature in the bone marrow.

120791.q: Where does the “B” in the name of B lymphocytes originally come from?
a: From the bursa of Fabricius in birds
120791.e: B cells were first discovered in chickens, where they mature in an organ called the bursa of Fabricius. The letter stayed, even though mammals do not have this organ.
120791.m: The “B” of B cells is a reminder of the bursa of Fabricius in birds.

120792.e: The B-cell receptor consists of an antibody anchored in the cell membrane. When it binds its antigen, the B cell is activated.
120792.m: The B-cell receptor is an antibody sitting in the membrane.

120793.q: What does a B cell become after it has recognised its antigen and been activated by a T helper cell?
120793.e: The activated B cell multiplies strongly. Some become plasma cells that make antibodies, others become long-lived memory cells.
120793.m: Activated B cells become plasma cells and memory cells.

120794.q: Why do people usually catch measles only once in their life?
a: The virus dies out after an illness
Afterwards the body makes no more mucous membranes
120794.e: After an infection, memory B cells and memory T cells stay in the body. At the next contact they react so quickly that you no longer fall ill.
120794.m: Memory cells often protect for life.

120795.q: What is the process called in which a B cell switches from making IgM to another antibody class such as IgA or IgE?
120795.e: In class switching, the constant part of the heavy chain is exchanged while the variable part stays the same. So the specificity is kept, but the function of the antibody changes.
120795.m: In class switching, an antibody keeps its target but changes its function.

120796.q: Which antibody class do B cells make first at the first contact with a germ?
120796.e: The early response to a new germ consists mainly of IgM. It is a large pentamer with ten binding sites and is good at clumping germs together.
120796.m: IgM is the first antibody of a new immune response.

120797.q: According to the clonal selection theory, how many different antigen structures is a single naive B cell specific for?
120797.e: Each B cell carries receptors with only one specificity. When it meets its antigen, it multiplies into a clone of identical cells.
120797.m: Each naive B cell recognises only one single antigen structure.

120798.q: Which mechanism creates the enormous variety of antibodies by recombining gene segments?
120798.e: As B cells mature, V, D and J gene segments are randomly put together in new ways. Susumu Tonegawa received the Nobel Prize in 1987 for this discovery.
120798.m: V(D)J recombination creates millions of different antibodies.

120799.q: From which cells do plasma cells develop?
120799.e: Activated B cells divide and develop into plasma cells. These are specialised in producing antibodies.
120799.m: Plasma cells are fully developed B cells.

120800.q: What is the main job of plasma cells?
a: They release large amounts of antibodies
120800.e: Plasma cells are real antibody factories. They release the antibodies into the blood and tissue fluids.
120800.m: Plasma cells produce antibodies in large amounts.

120801.q: Which cell organelle is especially well developed in plasma cells?
120801.e: Antibodies are proteins made for export on the ribosomes of the rough ER. Plasma cells therefore have an extensive rough ER and a large Golgi apparatus.
120801.m: The rough ER is where antibodies are produced in the plasma cell.

120802.q: Besides plasma cells, which cells develop from activated B cells and provide long-lasting immune protection?
120802.e: Some of the activated B cells become memory cells. At a new contact with the germ they react much faster, and this is also how vaccines work.

120803.q: Which cancer starts from abnormal plasma cells in the bone marrow?
120803.e: In multiple myeloma, a single clone of plasma cells multiplies out of control. It often produces large amounts of one uniform antibody and damages the bones.
120803.m: Multiple myeloma is a cancer of the plasma cells.

120804.q: Where are long-lived plasma cells mainly found in adults?
a: In the lens of the eye
120804.e: Long-lived plasma cells find special niches with survival signals in the bone marrow. From there they constantly release antibodies into the blood.
120804.m: Long-lived plasma cells live mainly in the bone marrow.

120805.q: What typical shape do the antibodies made by plasma cells have?
120805.e: An antibody consists of four protein chains that together form a Y. With its two arms it binds antigens, for example on germs.

120806.q: Roughly what share of the cells in the bone marrow are plasma cells in healthy adults?
120806.e: Plasma cells are only a small minority in healthy bone marrow. A clearly increased share is a sign of abnormal multiplication.
120806.m: Plasma cells are rare in healthy bone marrow.

120807.q: From which blood cells do macrophages develop?
120807.e: Monocytes circulate in the blood and move into tissues. There they mature into macrophages.
120807.m: Macrophages develop from monocytes in the blood.

120808.q: What does the Greek word “macrophage” mean?
120808.e: The word comes from the Greek “makros” for big and “phagein” for to eat. It describes the ability to take in large particles.
120808.m: Macrophages are the body's big eating cells.

120810.q: Which structure do macrophages form in tuberculosis to wall in germs?
120810.e: In tuberculosis, macrophages, giant cells and lymphocytes gather in small nodules around the bacteria. In this way the germs are walled in, but often not completely killed.
120810.m: Macrophages wall in tuberculosis bacteria in granulomas.

120811.q: How do macrophages recognise bacteria without having met them before?
a: By typical molecular patterns on the bacterial surface
By antibodies that they make themselves
120811.e: Receptors such as the Toll-like receptors recognise building blocks common to many germs, such as lipopolysaccharide. This is part of the innate defence.
120811.m: Macrophages recognise typical molecular patterns of germs.

120812.q: Apart from eating germs, what job do macrophages have?
a: They clear away cell debris and help wounds heal
120812.e: Depending on the signals, macrophages act more to promote inflammation (M1) or more to heal (M2). M2 macrophages clean up and promote the building of tissue.
120812.m: Macrophages fight germs and help with healing.

120813.q: Which macrophages clear away inhaled dust particles in the air sacs of the lungs?
120813.e: Alveolar macrophages move along the inner surface of the air sacs. They take in dust, soot and germs and are therefore also called dust cells.
120813.m: Alveolar macrophages keep the air sacs of the lungs clean.

120814.q: Which cells in the spleen mainly break down old red blood cells?
120814.e: Red blood cells live for about 120 days and then become less flexible. Macrophages in the spleen recognise and digest them, and the iron is recycled.
120814.m: Macrophages in the spleen dispose of old red blood cells.

120815.q: What, among other things, do macrophages use to kill bacteria they have taken in, inside the phagolysosome?
120815.e: An enzyme complex in the membrane produces superoxide and other aggressive oxygen compounds in the so-called respiratory burst. Together with enzymes and acid, they destroy the bacteria.
120815.m: Macrophages kill bacteria with aggressive oxygen compounds.

120816.q: Which part of the immune system does the complement system mainly belong to?
120816.e: The complement system consists of over 30 proteins in the blood plasma that can be activated without prior learning. But it works closely with antibodies.
120816.m: The complement system is part of the innate defence.

120817.q: With which part of the acquired defence does the complement system work closely?
120817.e: When antibodies stick to a germ, they can activate the complement system. This so-called classical pathway links the acquired defence with the innate defence.
120817.m: Antibodies can switch on the complement system.

120818.q: What does the complement system mainly consist of?
120818.e: The complement system includes over 30 proteins dissolved in the blood. They activate each other as in a cascade; one central protein is called C3.
120818.m: The complement system is a cascade of blood proteins.

120819.q: How does the complement system directly kill bacteria at the end of its cascade?
a: It makes holes in their membrane
It breaks them down with stomach acid
120819.e: Several complement proteins join together to form the membrane attack complex. Water flows in through this pore, and the bacterial cell bursts.
120819.m: The membrane attack complex punches holes in bacteria.

120820.q: What is it called when germs are marked with proteins such as C3b so that phagocytes can take them in more easily?
120820.e: C3b sticks to the surface of the germ. Phagocytes have receptors for it and therefore recognise marked germs much better.

120821.q: What effect do small fragments of the complement system such as C3a and C5a have?
120821.e: C3a and C5a widen blood vessels and attract immune cells. They are called anaphylatoxins; in large amounts they can contribute to shock.

120822.q: Why does the complement system have this name?
a: Because it complements the effect of antibodies
Because it is made of complex sugars
Because it only attacks complete cells
120822.e: At the end of the 19th century it was noticed that antibodies only dissolve bacteria together with a heat-sensitive factor in the serum. This complementing factor was therefore called “complement”.
120822.m: Complement adds to the effect of antibodies.

120823.q: Which symptoms typically occur in attacks in hereditary angioedema?
a: Severe swelling of the skin and mucous membranes
120823.e: In hereditary angioedema, a braking protein of the complement system, the C1 esterase inhibitor, is missing. Swellings develop that can become life-threatening in the larynx.
120823.m: In hereditary angioedema, the skin and mucous membranes swell up.

120824.q: What is the major histocompatibility complex also called in humans?
120824.e: In humans, the MHC molecules are called human leukocyte antigens, HLA for short. They were first detected on white blood cells.
120824.m: The human MHC is called the HLA system.

120825.q: What are MHC molecules on the surface of body cells for?
a: They show the immune system fragments of proteins
120825.e: MHC molecules present small pieces of proteins. T cells check these and so recognise whether a cell is infected or foreign.
120825.m: MHC molecules show the immune system what is inside a cell.

120826.q: Which cells carry MHC class I molecules?
a: Almost all body cells with a nucleus
120826.e: MHC class I molecules show fragments of proteins made inside the cell itself. Because almost every cell with a nucleus carries them, the immune system can detect infections almost everywhere.
120826.m: Almost every cell with a nucleus shows on MHC class I molecules what is going on inside it.

120827.q: What is HLA typing used for before a blood stem cell transplant?
a: To find the best possible matching donor
To determine the ABO blood group
120827.e: The better the HLA features match, the lower the risk of rejection and graft-versus-host disease. In Switzerland, Blood Transfusion Service SRC Switzerland keeps the register of blood stem cell donors.
120827.m: Matching HLA features are crucial for a stem cell transplant.

120828.q: Which feature of the HLA genes makes it hard to find a suitable unrelated donor?
a: Their position on the Y chromosome
120828.e: The HLA genes are among the most varied human genes, with thousands of known variants. That is why siblings are often a better match than unrelated people.
120828.m: HLA genes are extremely varied, which makes the search for a donor harder.

120829.q: What does the term histocompatibility mean?
120829.e: Histo means tissue, compatible means able to go together. The better the features of donor and recipient match, the better a transplant is tolerated.

120830.q: What can happen if the HLA features of a transplanted organ match the recipient poorly?
a: The immune system rejects the organ
The organ grows twice as fast
The organ becomes invisible to the immune system
120830.e: The immune system recognises foreign HLA features and attacks the organ. That is why matching donors are sought and medicines are given that damp down the immune system.
120830.m: Poorly matching HLA features lead to rejection.

120831.q: Which Swiss scientist shared the 1996 Nobel Prize with Peter Doherty for discovering that T cells only recognise antigens together with the body's own MHC molecules?
120831.e: Rolf Zinkernagel and Peter Doherty showed that cytotoxic T cells only kill virus-infected cells if these carry the matching MHC molecules. This principle is called MHC restriction.
120831.m: Rolf Zinkernagel discovered MHC restriction with Peter Doherty.

a: Messenger substances for communication between cells
Building blocks of the cell membrane
120832.e: Cytokines are small proteins that cells release to influence other cells. They control growth, inflammation and immune responses.
120832.m: Cytokines are the messenger substances of the immune system.

120833.q: How is fever useful during an infection?
a: It supports the defence and slows down many germs
120833.e: Cytokines turn up the set point for body temperature in the brain. The higher temperature makes immune cells more active and slows the multiplying of many germs.
120833.m: Fever helps the body fight germs.

120834.q: What is a life-threatening, excessive release of cytokines called?
120834.e: In a cytokine storm, immune cells release large amounts of messenger substances out of control. This can lead to high fever, circulatory failure and organ damage.
120834.m: A cytokine storm is a dangerous overreaction of the immune system.

120835.q: For which kind of illness are medicines used that block inflammation-promoting cytokines?
120835.e: In diseases such as rheumatoid arthritis or Crohn's disease, cytokines constantly drive the inflammation. Blocking them calms the inflammation down.
120835.m: Cytokine blockers slow down chronic inflammation.

120836.q: What are cytokines called that lure immune cells to a particular place?
120836.e: Chemokines form a concentration gradient that immune cells follow. This directed movement is called chemotaxis.
120836.m: Chemokines show immune cells the way.

120837.q: What does the name “interleukin” literally mean?
120837.e: The name came about because these messenger substances were first recognised as signals between white blood cells. Today we know that other cells make them too.
120837.m: Interleukins pass on signals between leukocytes.

120838.q: Which signs of inflammation are partly triggered by cytokines?
120838.e: Cytokines widen blood vessels and attract immune cells. As a result, the area becomes red, warm, swollen and painful.
120838.m: Cytokines help trigger the typical signs of inflammation.

120839.q: Where are white blood cells made?
120839.e: In the red bone marrow, all blood cells develop from stem cells. Cytokines such as growth factors control how many white blood cells are made.
120839.m: White blood cells are made in the bone marrow.

120840.q: Where do interferons get their name from?
a: Because they interfere with the multiplying of viruses
Because they develop in the inner ear
120840.e: The name comes from “interference”. Interferons slow down the multiplying of viruses in cells.
120840.m: Interferons interfere with the multiplying of viruses.

120841.q: Which Swiss researcher discovered interferons together with Alick Isaacs in 1957?
120841.e: In London, Jean Lindenmann and Alick Isaacs observed that cells treated with a virus release a substance that protects other cells from viruses. Lindenmann later became a professor at the University of Zurich.
120841.m: Jean Lindenmann was a co-discoverer of interferons.

120842.q: Which body cells can make interferon alpha and beta when they are attacked by a virus?
120842.e: Interferon alpha and beta belong to type I. Almost every body cell can make them as soon as it detects viral genetic material, and so it warns its neighbouring cells.
120842.m: Virus-infected cells release interferon alpha and beta.

120843.q: Which phagocytes are activated especially strongly by interferon gamma?
120843.e: Interferon gamma comes mainly from T cells and natural killer cells. It helps macrophages to kill the germs they have taken in more effectively.

120844.q: For which disease is interferon beta used as a long-term treatment?
120844.e: In relapsing multiple sclerosis, interferon beta can reduce the number of relapses. It was one of the first medicines that influence the course of this disease.
120844.m: Interferon beta is used for multiple sclerosis.

120845.q: For which viral infection was interferon alpha the standard treatment for a long time, before directly acting drugs arrived?
120845.e: Interferon alpha was usually given together with ribavirin for many months and had strong side effects. Today, directly acting antiviral tablets cure hepatitis C in most cases.
120845.m: Hepatitis C used to be treated with interferon alpha.

120846.q: How do type I interferons protect neighbouring cells from viruses?
a: They trigger the making of antiviral proteins there
They destroy viruses directly in the blood
120846.e: Interferons bind to receptors on neighbouring cells and switch on many genes there. The resulting proteins slow down, for example, the protein production of the viruses.
120846.m: Interferons put neighbouring cells into an antiviral state.

120847.q: Which side effect is especially common with interferon treatment?
120847.e: Interferons trigger the same signals as a viral infection. That is why people being treated often suffer from fever, aching limbs and tiredness.
120847.m: Interferons often cause flu-like side effects.

120848.q: Which cells make sure the body reacts faster at a second contact with a germ?
120848.e: After an infection, specific memory B and T cells remain. They recognise the germ again and quickly trigger a strong response.
120848.m: Memory cells remember germs that were fought before.

120849.q: Which antibody class dominates in the secondary response to a known germ?
120849.e: Memory B cells have usually already gone through class switching. In the secondary response, large amounts of high-affinity IgG antibodies are therefore made quickly.
120849.m: IgG antibodies dominate in the secondary response.

120850.q: What is a vaccination called in which the body makes antibodies and memory cells itself?
120850.e: In active immunisation, the body receives weakened or killed germs or parts of them. The immune system reacts and builds up a memory.
120850.m: In active immunisation, the immune system learns for itself.

120851.q: Why does passive immunisation not leave long-lasting protection?
a: It only works in the gut
120851.e: In passive immunisation, you receive ready-made antibodies, for example against tetanus. These are broken down after a few weeks, and no memory cells of your own are formed.
120851.m: Passive immunisation protects at once, but only for a short time.

120852.q: How does the secondary response differ in timing from the primary response?
120852.e: In the primary response it usually takes one to two weeks until there are many antibodies. In the secondary response a few days are enough, because memory cells are already waiting.
120852.m: The secondary response is faster and stronger than the primary response.

120853.q: Why does a measles vaccination usually protect for life, but a flu vaccination only for one season?
a: Flu viruses have no surface proteins
The flu vaccine contains no antigens
120853.e: Memory cells recognise a virus by its surface structures. In the measles virus these stay stable, while flu viruses keep changing them.
120853.m: Stable viruses allow a long immune memory.

120854.q: What is the indirect protection of unvaccinated people called when a large part of the population is immune?
120854.e: If the majority is immune, a germ hardly finds new hosts and does not spread. In this way people who cannot be vaccinated are also protected.
120854.m: Herd immunity also protects those who are not immune themselves.

120855.q: Why is a new flu vaccination needed almost every year despite immune memory?
a: The virus's surface proteins keep changing
Memory cells only live for one day
The vaccine only works in summer
120855.e: Through mutations, the haemagglutinin and neuraminidase of influenza viruses constantly change. This process is called antigenic drift, and the old antibodies then fit less well.
120855.m: Because of antigenic drift, the flu vaccine has to be updated regularly.

120856.e: Immunosuppression means that the defence is weakened, either on purpose or by disease. Doctors use it for transplants and autoimmune diseases.

120857.q: Why do people have to take immunosuppressants after an organ transplant?
a: So that the donor organ is not rejected
So that the organ grows faster
So that they do not get allergies
So that the blood becomes thicker
120857.e: The immune system recognises the foreign organ by its HLA features and would attack it. Immunosuppressants prevent this rejection reaction.
120857.m: Immunosuppressants protect a donor organ from rejection.

120858.q: Which important immunosuppressant was discovered at Sandoz in Basel in the 1970s?
120858.e: Ciclosporin comes from a soil fungus and was studied by researchers around Jean-François Borel at Sandoz. It made organ transplants much more successful.
120858.m: Ciclosporin from Basel revolutionised transplant medicine.

120859.q: Which immune cells mainly attack a donor organ during rejection?
120859.e: T cells recognise the foreign HLA features of the donor organ and attack it. Medicines such as ciclosporin and tacrolimus slow down their activation.
120859.m: During rejection, mainly T cells attack the donor organ.

120860.q: Which group of steroid hormones is often used to suppress inflammation and immune reactions?
120860.e: Glucocorticoids such as prednisone block the production of many inflammatory messenger substances. They are used, for example, for asthma, rheumatism and severe allergies.
120860.m: Glucocorticoids damp down inflammation and immune reactions.

120861.q: Which risk rises especially with long-term immunosuppression?
a: Blood sugar too high because of viruses
120861.e: Opportunistic germs are usually harmless for healthy people but can cause serious illness when the defence is weakened. Certain types of cancer also become more common.
120861.m: People who are immunosuppressed are especially prone to infections.

120862.q: What are diseases such as rheumatoid arthritis called, in which the immune system attacks the body's own tissue?
120862.e: In rheumatoid arthritis, the immune system attacks the inner lining of the joints. It is treated with medicines that damp down the immune system, such as methotrexate.
120862.m: In autoimmune diseases, the defence attacks the body itself.

120863.q: Why does chemotherapy often weaken the immune defence?
a: It damages fast-dividing cells in the bone marrow
It thins the blood with water
120863.e: Cytostatic drugs attack all rapidly dividing cells, including the blood-forming cells in the bone marrow. As a result, the number of white blood cells drops for a while.
120863.m: Chemotherapy weakens the defence because it hits the bone marrow.

120864.q: Which cells are most effective at activating naive T cells for the first time?
120864.e: Dendritic cells take up antigens in the tissue and present them in the lymph nodes. They carry especially many MHC and co-stimulatory molecules.
120864.m: Dendritic cells are the best starter cells for the T-cell response.

120865.q: What does a body cell infected with a virus show on its surface?
120865.e: Infected cells present pieces of the viral proteins on special molecules, the MHC molecules. In this way T cells can recognise that the cell is infected.
120865.m: Infected cells show the immune system fragments of the virus.

120866.q: Which T cells kill virus-infected cells that present a foreign antigen to them?
120866.e: Cytotoxic T cells, also called killer cells, recognise fragments of virus on the surface of infected cells. They then trigger the death of these cells.
120866.m: Killer T cells remove infected body cells.

120867.q: Why do T cells only recognise an antigen when another cell presents it to them?
a: Their receptor only binds fragments on MHC molecules
They have no receptors at all
They can only bind whole bacteria
120867.e: Unlike B cells, T cells do not recognise free germs. Their receptor only fits peptide pieces lying on the MHC molecules of a cell.
120867.m: T cells need a presented antigen.

120868.q: How do macrophages and dendritic cells take in whole bacteria before presenting parts of them?
120868.e: In phagocytosis, the cell flows around the bacterium with its membrane and digests it in a small vesicle. It then presents fragments of it on its surface.

120869.q: Which cells, once activated by an antigen-presenting cell, help B cells to make antibodies?
120869.e: T helper cells recognise a presented antigen and then release signals and messenger substances. In this way they stimulate matching B cells to make antibodies.
120869.m: T helper cells coordinate the immune response.

120870.q: What happens when a naive T cell recognises its antigen without a co-stimulatory signal?
120870.e: Without a second signal, the T cell switches into a state of unresponsiveness, called anergy. This protects against attacks on the body's own structures.
120870.m: Without co-stimulation, a T cell stays silent.

120871.q: Where do dendritic cells travel after taking up an antigen in the tissue?
120871.e: Through the lymph vessels, the dendritic cells reach the lymph node. There they meet many naive T cells and can activate the matching one.
120871.m: Dendritic cells carry antigens to the lymph nodes.

120872.q: Where do dendritic cells get their name from?
a: From being found in the teeth
120872.e: The Greek word dendron means tree. The cells have many tree-like branching extensions with which they capture and present antigens.
120872.m: Dendritic cells are named after their tree-like projections.

120873.q: In which unit is sound intensity given?
120873.e: Sound intensity is the sound power passing at right angles through an area, divided by that area. So its unit is W/m².
120873.m: Sound intensity is measured in watts per square metre.

120874.q: What sound power hits an area of 0.5 m² at right angles at an intensity of 10^-4 W/m²?
120874.e: Power is intensity times area: P = I · A = 10^-4 W/m² · 0.5 m² = 5 · 10^-5 W. So even loud noises carry only tiny amounts of power.
120874.m: Sound power is intensity times area.

120875.q: A point source radiates 1 W of sound power evenly in all directions. What is the intensity at a distance of 2 m?
120875.e: I = P / (4πr²) = 1 W / (4π · 4 m²) ≈ 0.0199 W/m². The power spreads over a sphere surface of about 50 m².
120875.m: The intensity is the power divided by the surface of the sphere.

120876.q: By what factor does the intensity of a point source fall if you triple the distance?
120876.e: The intensity is proportional to 1/r². At three times the distance you get 1/3² = 1/9.
120876.m: Three times the distance means one ninth of the intensity.

120877.q: How does the sound intensity change when the amplitude of oscillation of the air particles is doubled?
a: It becomes four times as great
It becomes eight times as great
120877.e: The energy of an oscillation is proportional to the square of the amplitude. So double the amplitude means 2² = 4 times the intensity.
120877.m: Sound intensity grows with the square of the amplitude.

120878.q: How does the total intensity change when two equally loud, independent sound sources run at the same time?
120878.e: With independent (incoherent) sources, the intensities add up. So two equal sources give twice the intensity.
120878.m: The intensities of independent sources are added.

120879.q: At roughly what sound level is the pain threshold of the human ear?
120879.e: A level of 120 dB corresponds to a sound intensity of about 1 W/m², which is a trillion times more than at the threshold of hearing. Such sound hurts and can damage hearing immediately.

120880.q: How is sound intensity defined in physics?
120880.e: Intensity tells you how much sound energy flows through an area of one square metre per second. So it describes a power density.
120880.m: Sound intensity is sound power per area.

120881.q: What is the sound intensity level of a sound with an intensity of 10^-6 W/m²?
120881.e: L = 10 · log10(I / I0) = 10 · log10(10^-6 / 10^-12) = 10 · 6 = 60 dB. That is roughly a normal conversation.
120881.m: Every factor of 10 in intensity adds 10 dB.

120882.q: Two independent sources each produce 90 dB and 80 dB on their own. Roughly what is the total level?
120882.e: You add the intensities: 10 · log10(10^9 + 10^8) = 10 · log10(1.1 · 10^9) ≈ 90.4 dB. The quieter source adds hardly anything.
120882.m: A source 10 dB quieter hardly raises the total level.

120883.q: By how much does the level rise when ten equally loud, independent sources run instead of one?
120883.e: The intensity becomes ten times as great. 10 · log10(10) = 10 dB.
120883.m: Ten times the intensity means 10 dB more.

120884.q: By how much does the sound level of a point source in a free field fall when the distance is doubled?
120884.e: The intensity falls to a quarter, and 10 · log10(1/4) ≈ -6 dB. This rule only applies without reflections.
120884.m: At double the distance, a point source loses about 6 dB.

120885.q: By how much does the sound pressure level rise when the sound pressure doubles?
120885.e: The sound pressure level is L = 20 · log10(p / p0). For a factor of 2, 20 · log10(2) ≈ 6 dB.
120885.m: Double the sound pressure gives about 6 dB more.

120886.q: What is A-weighting used for in values given in dB(A)?
a: It takes into account how the ear’s sensitivity depends on frequency
It converts the level into watts
It only applies to musical instruments
120886.e: The ear perceives low and very high notes more weakly than middle ones. The A filter weakens these ranges accordingly during measurement.
120886.m: A-weighting adapts measurements to human hearing.

120887.q: Roughly by how much must the level rise for a noise to seem twice as loud?
120887.e: As a rule of thumb for perceived loudness, 10 dB more seems about twice as loud. In physical terms, the intensity is ten times greater.
120887.m: About 10 dB more sounds twice as loud.

120888.q: What is the sound pressure level of a sound with an effective sound pressure of 0.2 Pa?
120888.e: L = 20 · log10(p / p0) = 20 · log10(0.2 Pa / 0.00002 Pa) = 20 · 4 = 80 dB. For sound pressure the factor 20 is in front of the logarithm, because intensity grows with the square of the pressure.
120888.m: For sound pressure level you use the factor 20 in front of the logarithm.

120889.q: In which unit is the loudness level given that refers to a 1 kHz tone perceived as equally loud?
120889.e: A tone has n phon if it seems as loud as a 1 kHz tone at n dB. So at 1 kHz, phon and decibel values are the same.
120889.m: The loudness level is given in phon.

120890.q: Who is the unit bel named after, of which the decibel is one tenth?
120890.e: The bel honours the telephone pioneer Alexander Graham Bell. In practice the decibel, one tenth of a bel, is usually used.
120890.m: A decibel is one tenth of a bel.

120891.q: What is the value of log10(1000)?
120891.e: 10³ = 1000. The base-10 logarithm gives the exponent, which is 3.
120891.m: The base-10 logarithm counts the powers of ten.

120892.q: By what factor does the measured ground motion amplitude rise when the magnitude of an earthquake is 1 higher?
120892.e: The magnitude scale is logarithmic: each step means ten times the amplitude. The energy released even rises by a factor of about 32 per step.
120892.m: One magnitude step more means ten times the amplitude.

120893.q: How many times more oxonium ions does a solution with pH 3 contain than one with pH 5?
120893.e: The pH value is the negative base-10 logarithm of the oxonium ion concentration. A difference of two pH steps gives 10² = 100.
120893.m: Each pH step corresponds to a factor of 10.

120894.q: Which law describes how a sensation grows roughly logarithmically with the strength of the stimulus?
120894.e: According to the Weber-Fechner law, multiplying a stimulus by ten always feels like roughly the same increase. That is why decibel scales are so practical for hearing.

120895.q: How many decades does the hearing range from 20 Hz to 20 kHz cover?
120895.e: A decade is a factor of 10. From 20 Hz via 200 Hz and 2 kHz to 20 kHz, there are three steps of ten.
120895.m: The human hearing range covers three decades.

120896.q: What level does an intensity have that is only one hundredth of the reference intensity?
120896.e: L = 10 · log10(0.01) = 10 · (-2) = -20 dB. Values below the reference value give negative levels.
120896.m: Intensities below the reference value have negative levels.

120897.q: In astronomy, what brightness factor corresponds to a difference of 5 magnitudes?
120897.e: The scale of apparent magnitude is set so that 5 magnitudes correspond exactly to a factor of 100. Smaller values mean brighter stars.
120897.m: Five magnitudes correspond to a brightness factor of 100.

120898.q: What does a sound level of 0 dB mean?
a: Roughly the threshold of hearing at 1 kHz
The pain threshold of the ear
120898.e: 0 dB is not an absence of sound but a reference value. It roughly corresponds to the quietest sound that a young, healthy person can just hear at 1 kHz.
120898.m: 0 dB is roughly the threshold of hearing, not complete silence.

120899.q: How large is the sound pressure at the threshold of hearing compared with normal air pressure?
120899.e: At the threshold of hearing, the air pressure varies by only about 20 micropascals, while air pressure itself is about 100,000 pascals. So the ear is an extremely sensitive measuring instrument.
120899.m: The ear detects the tiniest pressure changes.

120900.q: From what continuous sound level does the risk of permanent hearing damage rise clearly with long exposure?
120900.e: Anyone exposed to noise of 85 dB or more for long periods every day risks permanent hearing damage. That is why hearing protection is required at work from this level.
120900.m: From about 85 dB of continuous noise, hearing needs protection.

120901.q: Which frequency range is considered the hearing range of young, healthy people?
120901.e: Below about 20 Hz it is called infrasound, above about 20 kHz ultrasound. The upper limit falls with age.
120901.m: People hear from about 20 Hz to 20 kHz.

120902.q: Which frequencies are affected first by age-related hearing loss?
120902.e: In age-related hearing loss, it is mainly the sensory cells at the start of the cochlea, which process high notes, that are lost. So the threshold of hearing rises first at high frequencies.
120902.m: With age, you first hear high notes less well.

120903.q: What is the chart of the threshold of hearing in a hearing test called?
120903.e: In an audiogram, you mark for different frequencies how loud a tone must be for you to just hear it. This shows up hearing loss.
120903.m: An audiogram shows your personal threshold of hearing.

120904.q: What are curves called that join all the tones perceived as equally loud?
120904.e: Equal-loudness contours show what sound pressure level is needed at each frequency to perceive the same loudness. The lowest curve is the threshold of hearing.
120904.m: Isophones are curves of equal perceived loudness.

120905.q: How does the threshold of hearing at 50 Hz compare with 1 kHz?
120905.e: At low frequencies the ear is much less sensitive. A 50 Hz tone needs several dozen decibels more to be heard at all.
120905.m: Low notes must be louder for you to hear them.

120906.q: At roughly what sound level is the pain threshold of hearing?
120906.e: From about 130 dB, sound is not just heard but felt as pain. Such levels occur, for example, near jet engines.
120906.m: The pain threshold of hearing is at about 130 dB.

120907.q: What intensity does a sound level of 120 dB correspond to?
120907.e: I = I0 · 10^(L/10) = 10^-12 W/m² · 10^12 = 1 W/m². This value is twelve powers of ten above the threshold of hearing.
120907.m: A level of 120 dB corresponds to 1 watt per square metre.

120908.q: What is the effective sound pressure at a sound pressure level of 120 dB?
120908.e: p = p0 · 10^(L/20) = 20 µPa · 10^6 = 20 Pa. That is still very little compared with air pressure of about 100,000 Pa.
120908.m: Even very loud sound is only a small change in pressure.

120909.q: From what noise exposure level over a working day is noise at work considered dangerous to hearing according to Suva?
120909.e: Even a daily average from about 85 dB(A) can damage hearing in the long run, well below the pain threshold. Then hearing protection and other protective measures are required.
120909.m: Continuous noise can damage hearing from as little as 85 dB(A).

120910.q: What is hearing damage from a very short, extremely loud sound impulse called, for example a firecracker close to the ear?
120910.e: In acoustic trauma, a peak level lasting only a few milliseconds acts on the ear. It can immediately damage the sensitive sensory cells in the inner ear.
120910.m: A single very loud bang can damage hearing permanently.

120911.q: Which cells are destroyed in the inner ear by noise damage and do not grow back in humans?
a: The hair cells of the cochlea
The bone cells of the stirrup
The fat cells of the outer ear
120911.e: The hair cells turn vibrations into nerve signals. If they die, the hearing loss remains.
120911.m: Destroyed hair cells in the inner ear do not grow back.

120912.q: What is a whistling or rushing sound in the ear called, which can occur after a very loud concert, for example?
120912.e: Tinnitus is a noise in the ear without any outside sound source. It can occur temporarily or permanently after exposure to noise.
120912.m: Ear noises after loud sound are a warning sign from your hearing.

120913.q: Hearing protection reduces noise by 25 dB. What level reaches the ear in theory if it is 110 dB outside?
120913.e: Reductions in decibels are simply subtracted: 110 dB minus 25 dB = 85 dB. In practice the effect is often a little less if the protection does not fit well.
120913.m: The reduction in decibels is subtracted from the outside level.

120914.q: Why do noise barriers protect less well against low notes than against high ones?
a: Long waves are diffracted more over the edge
Low notes are amplified by air
120914.e: Diffraction at an edge is stronger the larger the wavelength is compared with the obstacle. So low notes get into the sound shadow more easily.
120914.m: Low notes travel around obstacles more easily.

120915.q: What is the Swiss ordinance called that sets exposure limits for road, rail and aircraft noise?
120915.e: The Noise Abatement Ordinance (LSV) is based on the Environmental Protection Act. It sets which noise levels are allowed in different zones.
120915.m: In Switzerland the Noise Abatement Ordinance sets the noise limits.

120916.q: Which exposure limit in the Swiss Noise Abatement Ordinance is the highest?
120916.e: The LSV has planning values, impact limit values and alarm values, rising in that order. If alarm values are exceeded, noise reduction is especially urgent.
120916.m: The alarm value is the highest limit in the Noise Abatement Ordinance.

120917.q: What is the maximum sound level averaged over one hour that events in Switzerland may reach (as of 2026)?
120917.e: Depending on the category chosen, the V-NISSG allows hourly levels of 93, 96 or at most 100 dB(A). In addition, the maximum level must never exceed 125 dB(A).
120917.m: At Swiss events, an hourly level of at most 100 dB(A) applies.

120918.q: Why does a heavy concrete wall block sound better than a light wooden wall of the same thickness?
a: Heavy walls are hardly set vibrating by sound
Concrete soaks up sound like a sponge
120918.e: The greater the mass of a wall, the more sluggish it is. Sound hardly makes it vibrate along, so less sound reaches the other side.

120919.q: What is the conversion of sound energy into heat in porous materials called?
120919.e: In absorption, the air particles rub in the fine pores and lose energy. Insulation, on the other hand, means that an obstacle mainly throws the sound back.
120919.m: Sound absorption turns sound into heat.

120920.q: Which building measure is especially effective at reducing footstep noise between flats?
120920.e: With a floating screed, the floor lies on an elastic insulating layer and does not touch the walls. So structure-borne sound is hardly passed on to the ceiling below.
120920.m: A floating screed separates the floor from the building.

120921.q: Which measure are Swiss authorities using more and more directly at the source against road noise?
120921.e: Low-noise surfaces have a finer, often porous surface and reduce the rolling noise of tyres. In the LSV, measures at the source take priority over noise barriers.
120921.m: Low-noise surfaces fight road noise at the source.

120922.q: How far away must a rock face be, at least, for you to hear an echo separately after at least 0.1 s (c = 343 m/s)?
120922.e: The sound travels there and back: d = c · t / 2 = 343 m/s · 0.1 s / 2 ≈ 17 m. Shorter delays merge with the original sound.
120922.m: For a clear echo you need a distance of several metres from the wall.

120923.q: What is the rapid, repeated echo between two parallel, smooth walls called?
120923.e: Between parallel sound-reflecting surfaces, sound travels back and forth several times. You hear a rapid, rattling echo.
120923.m: Parallel hard walls easily create flutter echoes.

120924.q: What is the sound absorption coefficient of an open window?
120924.e: Sound that escapes through the open window does not return to the room. So for the room, the window acts like a perfect absorber.
120924.m: An open window absorbs sound completely.

120925.q: What do diffusers do in recording studios and concert halls?
120925.e: Diffusers have an irregularly shaped surface and throw sound back in many directions. This avoids disturbing single reflections without deadening the room.
120925.m: Diffusers spread sound evenly around the room.

120926.q: What is the lowest room mode between two parallel walls 5 m apart (c = 343 m/s)?
120926.e: For the first axial mode, f = c / (2L) = 343 / 10 ≈ 34 Hz. At this frequency a standing wave forms between the walls.
120926.m: Room modes are standing waves between the walls.

120927.q: What is a room called whose walls reflect almost no sound?
120927.e: In anechoic chambers, the walls, ceiling and floor are covered with absorbing wedges. They are used to measure loudspeakers or microphones without the room affecting them.
120927.m: An anechoic chamber has practically no reverberation.

120928.q: What do you call a room in which you can clearly hear a whisper far away along a curved wall?
120928.e: On the curved wall, sound is reflected again and again at a shallow angle and stays close to the wall. A famous example is the Whispering Gallery of St Paul’s Cathedral in London.
120928.m: In a whispering gallery a curved wall carries the sound along.

120929.q: Which concert hall in Switzerland opened in 1998 and is known for its acoustics designed by the acoustician Russell Johnson?
120929.e: The concert hall in the Lucerne Culture and Convention Centre has electrically adjustable echo chambers. These allow the acoustics to be adapted to different works.
120929.m: The concert hall of the KKL Luzern is known for its adjustable acoustics.

a: The time until the level falls by 60 dB after switching off
The time until the first echo arrives from the back wall
The time sound needs to reach the opposite wall
The time of a single period of the tone
120930.e: The reverberation time T60 measures how long sound keeps ringing in a room. A drop of 60 dB means one millionth of the starting intensity.
120930.m: The reverberation time is the time to die away by 60 dB.

120931.q: Using Sabine’s formula T = 0.161 · V / A, what is the reverberation time of a room with a volume of 1000 m³ and an equivalent absorption area of 200 m²?
120931.e: T = 0.161 s/m · 1000 m³ / 200 m² = 0.805 s. That is a typical value for a lecture room.
120931.m: Large rooms with little absorption reverberate for a long time.

120932.q: Which physicist founded scientific room acoustics around 1900 with his formula for reverberation time?
120932.e: At Harvard University, Wallace Clement Sabine investigated why a lecture hall was hard to understand in. His findings were used in planning Boston Symphony Hall.
120932.m: Sabine is seen as the founder of modern room acoustics.

120933.q: According to Sabine, how does the reverberation time change if you double the equivalent absorption area?
120933.e: In Sabine’s formula, the absorption area A is in the denominator. So double the absorption means half the reverberation time.

120934.q: What reverberation time is typical for a large concert hall for symphonic music?
120934.e: For orchestral music, a full, carrying sound with about 2 s of reverberation is wanted. For speech, much shorter times are better.
120934.m: Concert halls have longer reverberation than lecture halls.

120935.q: What is the result of too long a reverberation time in a classroom?
120935.e: With long reverberation, syllables overlap and speech becomes unclear. Sound absorbers on the ceiling and walls make it easier to understand.
120935.m: Too much reverberation makes speech hard to understand.

120936.q: A wall of 50 m² has an absorption coefficient of 0.3. What is its equivalent absorption area?
120936.e: The equivalent absorption area is A = α · S = 0.3 · 50 m² = 15 m². It corresponds to an area that swallows sound completely.
120936.m: The equivalent absorption area is the absorption coefficient times the area.

120937.q: A room with a volume of 600 m³ is to have a reverberation time of 1.2 s according to Sabine (T = 0.161 · V / A). What equivalent absorption area is needed?
120937.e: Rearranged, A = 0.161 · V / T = 0.161 · 600 / 1.2 ≈ 80.5 m². This area must be reached with absorbers, people and furniture.
120937.m: Sabine’s formula lets you calculate the absorption needed.

120938.q: Waves travel at 440 m/s on a string 0.5 m long. What is the fundamental frequency of the string?
120938.e: The fundamental has a wavelength of 2L = 1 m. So f = c / (2L) = 440 m/s / 1 m = 440 Hz.
120938.m: The fundamental frequency of a string is wave speed divided by twice the length.

120939.q: What is the wave speed on a string with a tension of 100 N and a mass of 1 g per metre?
120939.m: Tighter and lighter strings carry waves faster.

120940.q: How does the fundamental frequency of a string change if you quadruple its tension?
120940.e: The frequency is proportional to the square root of the tension. √4 = 2, so the string sounds an octave higher.
120940.m: The frequency rises with the square root of the tension.

120941.q: A string has a fundamental of 200 Hz. What is the frequency of its 2nd overtone?
120941.e: The 1st overtone is the 2nd harmonic (400 Hz), the 2nd overtone is the 3rd harmonic. So 3 · 200 Hz = 600 Hz.
120941.m: The nth overtone is the (n+1)th harmonic.

120942.q: What is always found at the two fixed ends of a vibrating string?
120942.e: At the fixing points the string cannot move. So there are always nodes of the standing wave there.
120942.m: A string fixed at both ends has nodes at both ends.

120943.q: How does a thicker, heavier string of the same length and tension affect the pitch?
a: The note becomes louder, but not lower
120943.e: A greater mass per length lowers the wave speed. With the same length, this lowers the frequency.

120944.q: When playing a harmonic (flageolet), what happens if you only lightly touch a string in the middle?
a: The fundamental is missing and the second harmonic sounds
The string stops sounding at once and completely
Only the fundamental is clearly strengthened
A fifth below the fundamental sounds
120944.e: The light touch forces a node in the middle, which the fundamental does not have. What remains are vibrations with a node in the middle, so the second harmonic and its multiples.
120944.m: When playing a harmonic, a light touch of the finger forces a node.

120945.q: Which French scholar formulated the laws for the frequency of vibrating strings in the 17th century?
120945.e: Marin Mersenne described how the frequency depends on the length, tension and mass of the string. These relationships are called Mersenne’s laws.
120945.m: The laws of strings go back to Marin Mersenne.

120946.q: What is the wavelength of the fundamental of a guitar string with a vibrating length of 65 cm?
120946.e: In the fundamental, half a wavelength fits on the string. So λ = 2L = 2 · 0.65 m = 1.3 m.
120946.m: The wavelength of the fundamental is twice the string length.

120947.q: How are the frequencies of the partials of an ideal harmonic series related to the fundamental frequency?
120947.e: The partials have the frequencies f, 2f, 3f, 4f and so on. Such frequencies are called harmonic.
120947.m: The harmonic series consists of whole-number multiples of the fundamental frequency.

120948.q: What is the frequency of the 3rd partial of a 110 Hz fundamental?
120948.e: The 1st partial is the fundamental itself. The 3rd partial has three times the frequency: 3 · 110 Hz = 330 Hz.
120948.m: The nth partial has n times the fundamental frequency.

120949.q: What interval do the 2nd and 3rd partials of the harmonic series form?
120949.e: The frequency ratio is 3 : 2. This ratio corresponds to the perfect fifth.
120949.m: The ratio 3 to 2 gives a fifth.

120950.q: What interval lies between the 1st and the 4th partial?
120950.e: The frequency ratio is 4 : 1 = 2 · 2. Every doubling is an octave, so it is two octaves.
120950.m: The fourth partial is two octaves above the fundamental.

120951.q: What interval do the 4th and 5th partials form?
120951.e: The frequency ratio 5 : 4 corresponds to the pure major third. It is slightly lower than the major third in equal temperament.
120951.m: The ratio 5 to 4 gives a major third.

120952.q: What mainly determines the timbre of an instrument at the same pitch?
a: The strength of the individual overtones
120952.e: A violin and a flute can play the same fundamental. They still sound different because their overtones are of different strengths.

120953.q: Which woodwind instrument with an almost cylindrical bore mainly emphasises the odd-numbered partials in its low register?
120953.e: The clarinet behaves roughly like a cylindrical tube closed at one end. In such a tube, mainly the odd multiples of the fundamental frequency occur.
120953.m: The clarinet emphasises the odd partials.

120954.q: Which mathematical method can break a sound down into its individual sine waves?
120954.e: According to Joseph Fourier, every periodic oscillation can be written as a sum of sine waves. The result is the spectrum with fundamental and overtones.
120954.m: Fourier analysis shows the overtones of a sound.

120955.q: What interval do the 3rd and 4th partials form?
120955.e: The frequency ratio is 4 : 3. This ratio corresponds to the perfect fourth.
120955.m: The ratio 4 to 3 gives a fourth.

120956.q: What physical principle is active noise cancelling based on?
120956.e: A loudspeaker produces anti-noise that is the opposite of the unwanted noise. Crest and trough overlap and partly cancel each other out.
120956.m: Active noise cancelling wipes out sound with anti-noise.

120957.q: By how many degrees must the anti-noise be out of phase with the unwanted noise for cancellation to work best?
120957.e: With a shift of half a period, every crest meets a trough. If the amplitude is the same, the waves then cancel out.
120957.m: Anti-noise must be shifted by half a period.

120958.q: For which noises does active noise cancelling work best?
120958.e: Low notes have long wavelengths and change slowly, so the electronics can calculate the opposite signal in time. A typical example is the hum of jet engines or motors.
120958.m: Active noise cancelling works mainly on low humming.

120959.q: Which component do headphones with active noise cancelling use to pick up the unwanted noise?
120959.e: Small microphones pick up the surrounding sound. A signal processor uses this to calculate the antiphase signal for the loudspeaker.
120959.m: A microphone provides the signal for the anti-noise.

120960.q: In headphones with active noise cancelling, what mainly blocks the high frequencies?
a: The passive insulation of the ear cushions
120960.e: For high frequencies, active cancellation is difficult because the phase would have to be extremely precise. Tight ear cushions and the housing block these parts passively.
120960.m: Active and passive insulation work together in headphones.

120961.q: What is the method called in which a microphone on the outside of the headphones measures the noise before it reaches the ear?
120961.e: In the feedforward method, an outer microphone picks up the surrounding sound, and the electronics use it to calculate the anti-noise in advance. Many headphones combine this method with a microphone inside.
120961.m: In the feedforward method, the microphone sits on the outside of the headphones.

120962.q: In the feedback method of active noise cancelling, where is the microphone?
a: In the ear cup close to the loudspeaker
120962.e: In the feedback method, the microphone measures the remaining sound right in front of the ear. The electronics adjust the opposite signal so that this remaining sound is as small as possible.
120962.m: Feedback systems measure the remaining sound right at the ear.

120963.q: Apart from headphones, where else is active noise cancelling used?
120963.e: Some aircraft and cars use loudspeakers inside to reduce the low-frequency hum of propellers or engines. Pilot headsets work this way too.
120963.m: Active noise cancelling also quietens vehicle cabins.

120964.q: In which frequency range does medical ultrasound imaging typically work?
120964.e: Medical ultrasound devices usually use frequencies of about 2 to 15 MHz. These are far above the limit of human hearing.
120964.m: Ultrasound imaging works with ultrasound in the megahertz range.

120965.q: Which physical effect is used in the probe to produce and receive ultrasound?
120965.e: Piezo crystals deform when a voltage is applied, and so produce sound waves. In reverse, incoming echoes produce a measurable voltage.
120965.m: Piezo crystals turn voltage into ultrasound and back.

120966.q: What is the image in an ultrasound scan made from?
a: Echoes reflected at boundaries between tissues
120966.e: The probe sends out ultrasound and receives the echoes. From the strength and travel time of the echoes, the device builds up a greyscale cross-section image.
120966.m: An ultrasound image is made from the echoes in the tissue.

120967.q: An ultrasound echo returns after 130 µs. How deep is the reflecting boundary if the speed of sound is 1540 m/s?
120967.e: The sound travels there and back: d = c · t / 2 = 1540 m/s · 0.00013 s / 2 ≈ 0.10 m. The device calculates the image from the travel times.
120967.m: Ultrasound imaging measures depth from the travel time of the echoes.

120968.q: What speed of sound do ultrasound devices assume as standard for soft tissue?
120968.e: Most soft tissues carry sound in a similar way to water. So the devices use a single value of about 1540 m/s.
120968.m: Ultrasound devices calculate with about 1540 m/s in tissue.

120969.q: What is injected as a contrast agent in ultrasound imaging because it reflects ultrasound especially strongly?
120969.e: Tiny gas bubbles with a shell have a very different acoustic impedance from blood. They scatter the ultrasound strongly and so make the blood supply of organs visible.
120969.m: Microbubbles make blood vessels visible in ultrasound.

120970.q: What is the disadvantage of a higher ultrasound frequency?
120970.e: High frequencies give finer detail but are damped more strongly in tissue. So lower frequencies are used for organs lying deep inside.
120970.m: High ultrasound frequencies show detail but do not reach as deep.

120971.q: What advantage does ultrasound imaging have over X-rays and computed tomography?
a: It passes through bone especially well
It shows the air in the lungs best
120971.e: Ultrasound is a mechanical wave, not high-energy radiation. So the examination is considered gentle and can be repeated as often as needed.

120972.q: Why are air-filled lungs and bones hard to examine with ultrasound?
a: Because they reflect or damp the sound almost completely
Because they turn the ultrasound into light
Because they move too much during the measurement
Because their cells contain no water
120972.e: Air and bone have a very different acoustic impedance from soft tissue. So the ultrasound can hardly get behind them, and an acoustic shadow forms.
120972.m: Behind air and bone, ultrasound shows a shadow.

120973.q: What does a diversity index measure in ecology?
a: The number of species and how individuals are distributed among them
Only the total number of all individuals
The biomass of the largest species
The area of a nature reserve
120973.e: A diversity index combines the number of species and the evenness of the distribution of individuals in a single number. Two communities with the same number of species can therefore differ in diversity.
120973.m: A diversity index takes into account the frequency distribution as well as the number of species.

120974.q: What is the simple number of species in an area called?
120974.e: Species richness only counts how many species occur. How common each species is does not matter.
120974.m: Species richness counts the species without considering how common they are.

120975.q: Which term describes how evenly the individuals are distributed among the species present?
120975.e: Evenness (equitability) is greatest when all species are equally common. If one species strongly dominates, evenness is low.
120975.m: Evenness measures how evenly the species are distributed.

120976.q: What does the Simpson index D, as the sum of the squared proportions (Σ p²), indicate?
a: The probability that two randomly drawn individuals belong to the same species
The average body size of the species
120976.e: If you draw two individuals at random (with replacement), Σ p² is the probability that both belong to the same species. A high value therefore means low diversity.
120976.m: A high Simpson value Σ p² means that a few species dominate.

120977.q: A meadow has three species with proportions of 0.5, 0.25 and 0.25. What is the Simpson diversity 1 − Σ p²?
120977.m: You get the Simpson diversity by subtracting Σ p² from 1.

120978.q: According to Robert Whittaker, what is the diversity within a single habitat called?
120978.e: Whittaker distinguished alpha diversity (within a habitat), beta diversity (difference between habitats) and gamma diversity (whole region).
120978.m: Alpha diversity describes the variety at a single site.

a: The difference in species composition between habitats
The number of species in a whole region
The genetic variety of a species
The number of individuals per square metre
120979.e: Beta diversity measures the species turnover between sites. If two meadows have completely different species, it is high.
120979.m: Beta diversity measures how much habitats differ in their species.

120980.q: Which three levels of biodiversity are usually distinguished?
a: Genetic diversity, species diversity, ecosystem diversity
Cell diversity, organ diversity, species diversity
Plant diversity, animal diversity, fungus diversity
Climate diversity, soil diversity, water diversity
120980.e: Biodiversity includes the variety of genes within species, the variety of species and the variety of habitats and ecosystems. This is also how the Convention on Biological Diversity defines it.
120980.m: Biodiversity includes genes, species and ecosystems.

120981.q: What does the Shannon index measure in ecology?
a: Species diversity, taking into account how common each species is
Only the number of species in an area
The total biomass of an area
The growth rate of a population
120981.e: The Shannon index takes into account not only how many species occur but also how evenly the individuals are distributed among them. The higher the value, the more diverse the community.
120981.m: The Shannon index combines the number of species and how common they are.

120982.q: Which field does the Shannon index originally come from?
120982.e: Claude Shannon developed the measure in 1948 as entropy in information theory. Ecology later adopted it as a measure of diversity.
120982.m: The Shannon index comes from Claude Shannon’s information theory.

120983.q: What is the Shannon index (natural logarithm) for two equally common species?
120983.e: With p = 0.5 for both species, H = −2 · 0.5 · ln 0.5 = ln 2 ≈ 0.693.
120983.m: For S equally common species, the Shannon index equals ln S.

120984.q: What is the Shannon index of an area where only a single species occurs?
120984.e: With p = 1, ln 1 = 0, so H = 0. A monoculture has no diversity in the sense of the index.
120984.m: A single species gives a Shannon index of zero.

120985.q: For a given number of species S, when does the Shannon index reach its maximum?
a: When all species are equally common
When the number of individuals is at its maximum
120985.e: With equal proportions, the uncertainty about which species you will draw next is greatest. The maximum is then Hmax = ln S.
120985.m: The Shannon index is greatest when species are equally common.

120986.q: What does the evenness of a community describe?
a: How evenly the individuals are distributed among the species
How many species occur in total
How large the area studied is
120986.e: Evenness, for example according to Pielou, compares the measured Shannon index with the maximum for equally common species. It lies between 0 and 1; 1 means that all species are equally common.
120986.m: Evenness shows how evenly the species are represented.

120987.q: Two meadows each have three species. In meadow A all species are equally common; in meadow B one species makes up 90 per cent. Which meadow has the higher Shannon index?
a: Both the same, as the number of species is the same
Meadow B, because one species dominates
120987.e: For the same number of species, the Shannon index is highest when all species are equally common. If one species strongly dominates, the index falls considerably.
120987.m: Unequal proportions push the Shannon index below its maximum.

120988.q: What is the maximum Shannon index (ln) for four species?
120988.e: The maximum is ln 4 ≈ 1.386. It is reached when each species has a proportion of 0.25.
120988.m: The highest possible Shannon index is the natural logarithm of the number of species.

120989.q: Who coined the concept of biodiversity hotspots in 1988?
120989.e: The British environmental scientist Norman Myers described areas with many endemic plants and severe habitat loss in 1988. Conservation International later developed the concept further.
120989.m: Norman Myers invented the concept of biodiversity hotspots in 1988.

120990.q: What does it mean if a plant species in a hotspot is endemic?
a: It occurs naturally only in this area
It was brought in by humans
It is found all over the world
120990.e: Endemic species exist only in a particular area. Hotspots have especially many of them, so losing them there would be irreplaceable.
120990.m: Endemic species occur only in a particular area.

120991.q: Apart from having many endemic species, which second criterion must a biodiversity hotspot meet?
a: It has lost at least 70 per cent of its original vegetation
It lies completely in the tropics
It is larger than one million square kilometres
120991.e: Hotspots are not only especially rich but also especially threatened. That is why at least 70 per cent of the original habitats must have been lost.
120991.m: A hotspot is rich in species and at the same time severely threatened.

120992.q: Where are most of the Earth’s biodiversity hotspots?
a: In the deserts of Central Asia
120992.e: Most hotspots are in warm regions with many endemic plants, such as the tropical Andes, Madagascar or South-East Asia. Habitat loss is also great there.
120992.m: Most hotspots are in the tropics and subtropics.

120993.q: What proportion of the Earth’s land surface do the hotspots still cover (intact vegetation)?
120993.e: The remaining intact habitats of the hotspots cover only about 2.5 per cent of the land surface. Even so, more than half of all plant species live there as endemics.
120993.m: A large part of plant diversity is concentrated on a tiny part of the land surface.

120994.q: Which of these areas is a recognised biodiversity hotspot in Europe?
120994.e: The Mediterranean Basin is a hotspot because of its many endemic plants and its long use by humans. It is one of the largest in the world.
120994.m: The Mediterranean Basin is Europe’s best-known biodiversity hotspot.

120995.q: Why were hotspots proposed as a tool for nature conservation?
a: To use scarce funds where the most species per area can be saved
To steer tourists into nature reserves
To count the number of species worldwide exactly
120995.e: The concept helps to set priorities: investing in hotspots protects many irreplaceable species on a small area. Critics complain that animals and less species-rich ecosystems lose out.
120995.m: Hotspots help to use conservation money as effectively as possible.

120996.q: Which island, together with neighbouring islands, is a hotspot of its own and famous for its lemurs?
120996.e: Madagascar separated from other land masses over 80 million years ago. This produced a great many endemic species, including all the lemurs.
120996.m: Madagascar is a hotspot with an extremely large number of endemic species.

120997.q: What is a young endemic species called that has not yet been able to spread further since it arose?
120997.e: Neoendemics arose only a short time ago, for example on islands or in lakes. Their small range is a result of their young age.
120997.m: A neoendemic is a young species with a still narrow range.

120998.q: What is the opposite of an endemic species called, that is, a species found almost worldwide?
120998.e: Cosmopolitan species such as the housefly or bracken occur almost everywhere on Earth. Endemics, by contrast, are narrowly restricted.
120998.m: A cosmopolitan species is found almost all over the world.

a: An old species that now survives only in a remnant area
A young species that has only just arisen
An extinct species known as a fossil
A species newly introduced by humans
120999.e: Palaeoendemics used to be more widespread and have survived only in a refuge.
120999.m: Palaeoendemics are remnants of species that used to be more widespread.

121000.q: Why are there particularly many endemic species on remote islands?
a: The climate on islands is always tropical
Islands have no predators and no diseases
Endemic species are deliberately released on islands
121000.e: A few species that arrived continue to evolve without gene exchange with the mainland. This produces new species found only there, such as Darwin’s finches on the Galápagos Islands.
121000.m: Isolation promotes the formation of endemic species.

121001.q: Which seal species is endemic to a freshwater lake in Siberia?
121001.e: The Baikal seal lives only in Lake Baikal and is one of the few freshwater seals. The lake is home to many other endemic species.
121001.m: The Baikal seal occurs only in Lake Baikal.

121002.q: Which group of fish has produced many endemic species in Swiss lakes?
121002.e: In the Swiss lakes north of the Alps, numerous whitefish species arose after the last ice age, often living in just one lake. Some of them disappeared when many lakes were over-fertilised in the 20th century.
121002.m: Many endemic whitefish species live in Swiss lakes.

121003.q: Why are endemic species particularly threatened with extinction?
a: Their small range can be lost through a single disturbance
They basically only reproduce once in their lives
They are always very large animals
